title: Sandokai Part 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett returns to the Sandokai, "The Merging of Difference and Unity," the eighth-century poem by Shitou on page eleven of the chant book, and takes up its second page on light and dark. Nomon tells of the Dalai Lama greeting an exhausted new arrival from Tibet, joking one moment and weeping with her the next, as an example of joy and sorrow held together. Einstein's passage calling separateness an "optical delusion of consciousness" joins the poem's image of the front and back foot in walking. Nomon reads through the closing lines on mountains and rivers and on not passing days and nights in vain, then sends everyone into groups of three to speak about the light and dark in their own lives.

It's the tenth.
I'm getting used to my graduated glasses.

Something's wrong with the light and the book?
I never had glasses.
I have had readers, and I was taking them off and putting them on, taking them off and putting them on.

So now I can see you, and the notes.
Wow.
I hold my head the right way.
You have to be a little more like a bird, I've noticed.
I appreciated, well, I appreciate a lot of things, but one of the things I appreciated was Mari's invitation to come to dokusan, to private interview, which is a core practice in Zen.
The word dokusan is two characters.
Most of the words that are used are two characters.
And it means something pretty close to "come alone," which is strange, actually.
But there's another person sitting there, so what's that about?
What it's about, I think, is that the job of the teacher and of the situation of the private interview (interview is not even the right word) is for us to help each other in meeting ourselves.
To go alone, to really meet yourself.
And not the usual self that we worry about and fret over and are upset by and occasionally very excited by, and mostly not.
To meet some other self, some deeper self, some kind of true self.
So the teacher, unless they either have psychic powers or are a narcissist, can't look inside your head and see what that is exactly.
Some of the Zen stories kind of sound that way.

But a teacher who's practiced for a while, and has practiced holding the space and sitting in the seat and being present and not getting too lost in their small self, can sometimes support a situation for both people.

I feel like what happens in dokusan that's really helpful is not anything that one person says and the other person answers, but something that emerges in the middle, something that happens organically, something that Buddha makes happen.
We don't make it happen.
And it's not always so flashy.
Sometimes it feels very ordinary.
But probably when you leave the dokusan room, you feel different.
Some little something happened, and it's an important something.
So I just want to make sure everyone knows you're fully invited.
In a way, it's really nice of us to have it be that you get to initiate: okay, I'm going to go, I put my little card out.
But in a way, it would be nicer if we just required everyone to go, because then you wouldn't have to decide, right?
Am I allowed?
Am I good enough?
Do I have a good question?
Is the teacher any good?
I don't know, right?
So anyway, long story short, stick your card out and we'll see what happens.
Also, don't worry, there's no need to try to manage the situation.
Sometimes people do this.
They look around and say, oh, there's a couple of people with their cards out.
Are we covering?
No.
You don't have to do that.
You can trust the system to organize it.
If there's more people than there's time, then next time.
And you never know.
The meetings are brief, and sometimes more people can be seen, sometimes less.
So anyway, I thought that was nice, the way Mari said everyone's invited.
There's no status, and you don't have to come here for a year.
There's no secret handshake or anything like that.
It's just for two conditioned humans to meet as Buddhas and see what happens.
We'll see.
So the actual topic of tonight's talk is the second talk in a row, part two.
If you missed part one, it's okay.
It's on a Zen poem that's in our chant book called The Merging of Difference and Unity, so it may be helpful to be looking at it.
I never seem to remember to bring myself a chant book.
Somebody has to jump up, sorry.
What page is it on?
Somebody have it out?
Eleven.
Page eleven.
It was written in the 700s by a Chinese Zen teacher.
They would say chan, not zen, just different pronunciations of the same thing.
It's to encourage us around this same question of experiencing our true selves, experiencing our true world.
Not the one that we have concocted in our heads.
We come by it honestly, right, through our education and our upbringing.
But it's something deeper than that and truer than that, and beyond what we can quite think about.
Last week we looked at the first page, so let's just briefly breeze through it.
It's good for all of us, and especially if you weren't here.
The first part is sourcing the teachings with the Buddha, this first paragraph about the great sage of India.
Just like I was trying to say about dokusan, it's not about how good you are, how smart you are, how much you studied.
It's true for everybody, sharp or dull, whether you're from the north or the south or anywhere.
Then the second paragraph talks a little bit about obstacles.
It talks about grasping.
It talks about trying so hard to figure things out.
It talks about how it's right in front of us but it's hard for us to see and understand.
And then it goes on to say that really and truly it's not something where you're going to have a great epiphany one day when you're reading, when you're thinking.
It may come to you through an ordinary moment with your ordinary senses.
There are many Zen stories like that.
And then all this is happening in an elemental universe, a universe of earth and wind and water and fire.
Even though we've since concocted a lot of other understandings of the physical universe, these are still beautiful and important for us.
Then our assignment, the last paragraph there on the first page, is to really tune in: to open our eyes, our ears, our nose, our tongues, and to notice everything that arises, carefully and fully.
There's no unimportant stuff in saying this.
There's no unimportant stuff.
Sometimes contemporary mindfulness teachers say, what happens when you are tuned out?
Or Zen teachers could say this too, I guess.
Anybody could say this.
What happens when you miss a moment?
Well, you just missed your life.
This is our lives.
Don't miss them.
I like all poetry.
There's some imagery and metaphor which is not explained.
There's an interesting image towards the bottom of page eleven about a tree.
One way to look at it might be that we're all part of the same great tree, a great tree of life.
It all shares some essence, some deep connection.
The roots are deep in the earth, but we're different expressions of it, different leaves, different branches of the same tree.
The last phrase there, *each has its own speech*: we each have our own expression.
So in the title of the poem, I didn't really talk about that too much, but it's merging of difference and unity.
There's a unity to all being the tree, and there's difference.
If you look carefully at a physical tree, this is true.
The leaves are very similar.
You can tell this is a birch leaf, this is a cedar leaf, this is a Douglas fir needle.
But if you look really closely, you see that no two are the same.
They're different.
So then the second page, and he kind of foreshadowed this, has the metaphor of light and darkness.
This is the most important and most famous part of this little poem, so let me say a little bit about that.
The first paragraph is just a couple of lines in English, and we could study this for a long time.
*In the light there is darkness, but don't take it as darkness.
In the dark there is light, but don't see it as light.*
This doesn't seem too out there.
We think today about the dark and the light.
It's through our language and through how we talk about what's going on in the world and in our lives.
We talk about light and darkness in all kinds of ways.
Some of these human things, I think, have always been true and always will be true.
How ancient and how universal to think about the light and the dark.

The core thing that Zen tries to help us see, though, and this poem is trying to help us see and study this, is that we can get a little messed up by our language, the way our language always operates in opposites.
They need each other, but they don't exactly have the meaning that we always think they do.
Take tall and short.
You can't have tall without short or short without tall.
Everything is radically relative, right?
We know this.
But it's wired into us through our language and our thinking, dividing everything always into this and that, and that and this, me and you, light and dark.
So he's saying here, don't think they're quite so separate.
The first line, in the light there is darkness, actually has the Chinese character for middle or central right in the middle of it, which didn't quite make the cut in the English.
So right in the middle, interwoven, intertwined, in the light is darkness.
It's not like, it's really bright in here, I'm going to find a dark corner.
There's darkness in the light itself.
The light has the nature of darkness.
"But don't take it as darkness" is interesting.
Don't think that there is some simple way to then turn your dualism into just a new dualism.
Merging of difference and unity: it's light-dark, it's dark with light.
It's light, it's dark.
So our question in the end, at some point with these traditional texts, is always, well, how do we practice with this?

One of the things the original Buddha is famous for saying is, people would ask him abstract philosophical questions, what's the nature of the universe kind of stuff, and usually he'd refuse to answer.
One of his answers is, "I only talk about suffering and the end of suffering."
In other words, the rest of it is just spinning your wheels, which sounds kind of anti-philosophical.
There are layers and layers of Buddhism.
It's probably better to say Buddhisms, plural, than Buddhism, because the different schools do have some differences to them.
And some unity, right?
So it's all one tradition in the end.
I would say in our broad school of Buddhism, which is called Mahayana, there is philosophy, absolutely.
You can't argue with that.
There's plenty of philosophy.
Like you can apply the duck test: if it quacks like a duck, you know what I mean?
It's also religion.
If you're trying to avoid religion by coming to Zen, sorry.
The duck test also turns up religion pretty clearly.
But anyway, you seem to have some philosophy.
In the end it's a both-and.
It also must be a path to liberation, a way to freedom from suffering, or maybe more accurate to say freedom in suffering, since suffering can't exactly be avoided.
But there's suffering, and then there's suffering.
So how do we practice with this?
Well, maybe a simple way to take this metaphor of light and dark is just the usual way.
Nothing wrong with that.
Our usual minds tend to prefer the light, right?
We want to be happy.
We like being energized and excited and connected and fired up.
Yippee.
But we know through experience that there's something sort of unsustainable and flimsy about that.
Incomplete.
Somehow it seems like you also need the darkness, don't you think?
Yeah, you need the darkness.
There's that part of us that's kind of yeah-but about that, right?
Like, yeah.
Do I really?
So that's one way of practicing with this.
It's to be a little lighter about trying so hard, which is what our mind is doing, to divide happiness from sadness, joy from sorrow.
Are they actually so separate?
And if you pay a lot of attention to your feelings, I think you're already seeing, maybe not.
Maybe feelings that seem to be opposites of each other actually can be present at the same time and together.
And maybe in some mysterious way, they support each other.
So maybe happiness that feels the sadness in the middle is a stronger, clearer, and more thorough and complete happiness.
And then when we're sad, there's some joy there, somehow, too.
One simple way of thinking about this is just through things I've read, maybe you've read, too, about some of our great practitioners, like His Holiness the Dalai Lama.
This is a story I read one time that stuck with me so strongly.
His Holiness is in his meeting rooms in Dharamsala in northern India, where he lives in exile with the Tibetan community.
And he's having a good time.
He's talking about the Dharma.
He's joking around with somebody.
If you've ever seen any images or video of him, he laughs a lot.
He jokes around.
He giggles.
He's one of our greatest Buddhist practitioners in all the world, and he's a good giggler.
It's a sweet little film, and it's a film and a book also about His Holiness's friendship with Archbishop Desmond Tutu of South Africa that we're checking out.
Those guys would just goof around, and they both, as we know, have seen incredible suffering.
Countries destroyed by hatred and division, when people hurt so deeply.
Anyway, back to the story.
His Holiness is in a typical morning in his life, and he's already, by the way, up at three to practice for five hours every day.
So we have something to aspire to there.
Then a new arrival from Tibet is ushered in.
I think of it as a woman or maybe a family, and they're bedraggled and exhausted.
You can just tell they've been through hell.
Because people still, to this day, sometimes manage to walk out of Tibet into northern India.
It's an enormous journey, like weeks or something, through high passes, and I'm sure people die on the way.
And His Holiness goes to greet her and is instantly with her, crying, feeling the sorrow and the pain of losing their country and the oppression and hurt that he knows she has seen.
He doesn't know the details yet, but he knows.
And he's connecting deeply.
So, joy and sorrow.
The Chinese psychology person call it affective flexibility, but that's not quite the whole thing.
It's not just flexibility between this and that.
It's feeling the interconnection and integration of all the feelings, all the emotions.
So, light and dark, light and dark.
And then it seems like it just flips the other way.
The Chinese has a little variation here, which is interesting.
*In the dark there is light, but don't see it as light.
Take it as darkness.* It uses a character that means something like, instead of "take it," it means perceive it.
It's hard to explain and I don't really know the Chinese well enough, but it's not quite "take it," it's more like understand it or feel it.
*Don't feel it as darkness* is probably a little closer.
But in *in the dark there is light*, it does use the character for "to see": *don't see it as light.* Maybe it's because light is the thing we see.
It's an encouragement to go deeper there.
You don't just see the light.
Maybe you feel the light.
Other quirky Zen teachings talk about hearing sights and seeing sounds in the same kind of way.
And in both of them, the same character.
And it's a character that looks like it should be in the middle.
I can share the Chinese if we have time in a minute.
It's all right in the middle: not off to the side, not hiding under a rock.
Right in the middle of our light is our darkness.
Right in the middle of our darkness is our light.
And it's not exactly ours either.
It's just a way of talking.
That is a kind of trick of consciousness.
We come by it honestly, like I always try to remind myself: it's okay.
Of course we think in this way, to think that light and dark are so separate, and one is good and one is bad.
All this made me think of a famous quote by Albert Einstein, of all people.
One of the few quotes by him I know.
I'm sure he's said a lot of other things.
The quote is:
*A human being is a part of a whole, called by us "universe," a part limited in time and space.*
He used gendered language.
I'll just clean it up, though.
*They experience themselves, their thoughts and feelings, as something separate, something separated from the rest.
This is a kind of optical delusion of their consciousness.
The separateness.
This delusion is a kind of prison for us, restricting us to our personal desires and to the affection for a few persons nearest to us.
Our task must be to free ourselves from this prison by widening the circle of compassion to embrace all living creatures and the whole of nature in its beauty.*
Isn't that wonderful?
Who would have thought that theoretical physicists would talk that way?
And I've checked.
I'm going to be careful these days: any quote you get by Einstein, Buddha, anybody is probably fake.
We've got to always look them up.
So our separateness is an optical delusion of consciousness and a kind of prison for us.
Not even a kind of: it is our central prison, right?
Our separateness, and how it limits us.
Our task must be to free ourselves from this prison by widening our circle of compassion to all creatures and the whole of nature in its beauty.
And I think the way to do that task, which he doesn't say, is to see through this optical delusion of consciousness, to see through this separateness.
In the light there is dark, in the dark there is light, right in the middle.
In me there is you, in you there is me, right in the middle.
And it's not something we can exactly figure out with our heads.
Our heads do tend to dominate, at least mine does.
Probably some people here are a little more body and heart centered, which is great, lucky for you, because I think it's something we feel.
Sometimes the word "appreciate" is used: we learn, we start to appreciate.
Sometimes, like in the stories, there's an aha moment, but often not.
It's more like it just sneaks up on you.
Maybe you don't even notice that you're not treating others quite so separately.
You're not dividing yourself up in quite the same ways that you used to.
Maybe you're just a little more relaxed, a little more happy, a little less uptight.
And this is seeing through that optical delusion in some way.
You're more willing to feel what you're feeling, and not locking it down by how you think about it and talk about it, just feeling it.

Then, to help us make sense of all this, and this is part of why I made a little bit of a big deal of walking meditation today, the author, whose name sounds something like Schürtel, uses the metaphor of walking to help us understand the non-dualness of these dualities.
*Light and dark oppose one another like the front and back foot in walking.*
Isn't that beautiful?
You do have two separate feet, you can see that.
But it's kind of ridiculous to say you have two separate feet, right?
If you had two separate feet, your right foot could end up over there and your left foot over there, and where are you?
So the two feet are always one body, and they're two feet.
And it's really great: one's in front, one's behind, and then the other one's front.
So it's not exactly a front foot and a back foot, but there are.
There are and there aren't.
It's fluid and it's constantly changing.
So this is a beautiful, beautiful metaphor, I think, for this.
Just watch our walking and appreciate how rich that actually is.
And the rest of the poem, I think, is pretty straightforward, which doesn't mean it's not profound and useful.
So let's just read through it, and then I'm excited to have some time to discuss together what you think about light and dark in your own life.
*Each of the myriad things has its merit, expressed according to function and place.*
Myriad things means dharmas.
Each of the dharmas has its merit.
So everything matters, right?
There's nothing that doesn't matter.
There's no write-offs.
But it matters conditionally and relationally, according to function and place.
And it's just as it should be.
So here we're talking about a Mahayana concept, sometimes called, which is hard to understand, but here's a great description of it.
*Phenomena exist, box and lid fit.*
The way things just are.
The is-ness of things: yeah, box and lid fit.
*Principle responds.*
If you were here last Sunday, we had one of our senior students, Bob Rose, talking about Bodhidharma.
It's great teachings on principles.
So this is actually the same character.
It all responds.
There's nothing wrong with our ideas and our philosophy and our principle, but it doesn't exist on its own.
It responds to what is.
*When the arrow points meet.*
It shows up in another Zen poem we chant: the arrow points meet.
So just this, right here, right here.
And then we have some practical advice.
*Hearing the words, understand the meaning.*
So we have to practice our whole lifetime to try to understand more clearly what's happening, what we're being offered.
We can never write anything off, never be like, "Oh, I don't get it, moving on."
No, we understand, we learn, we listen again, we ask.
*Hearing the words, understand the meaning.* So, learn to understand the meaning, you could say, too.
And then we have great advice for all of us, and especially in the Zen setting.
*Don't set up standards of your own.*
It's a little bit double-edged for us in the 21st century, and probably all centuries.
*Don't set up standards on your own.* So does this mean we're just passive and accept what everyone tells us?

I was thinking earlier, I definitely identified when I was younger as a non-conformist, and we all learned how to say the word "anti-disestablishmentarianism," because it was like the longest word or something.
I forgot all about that.
It just popped into my head today: anti-disestablishmentarianism.
Ridiculous.
We were all, like, 16-year-old brilliant philosophers.
So we do need to think for ourselves, for sure, but something is lost if we let our separated self, lost in that optical delusion of consciousness, think it can figure it all out and knows best.
Maybe the metaphor of a recipe is good.
Our elders, our traditions offer us some recipes.
Probably good to cook from the recipe at first, see how it comes out, and then start making it your own.
And similarly, the next line is basically the same thing again.
*If you don't understand the way right before you, how will you know the path as you walk?*
So there's a lot of humility suggested here.
The egoistic self always thinks it knows where it's going, right?
It makes its own standards and knows the path.
But do we really know where we're going?
*How will you know the path as you walk?* So we have a lot to learn.
And, and, we already know.
So something here about deeply trusting that true sense of how it is, and being willing to push back when that's what's called for.
How do we know?
A lifetime question, for sure.
For me, it's good to start by listening and then see.
*Progress is not a matter of far or near, but if you are confused, mountains and rivers block your way.*
So you will always be you.
This is not about some future time and some future place where you'll be a different you or a better you or improved in some way, free from all your whatevers.
It's not about going somewhere far or being right where you are.
It's not about far or near.
But if you're confused, if you're grasping, if you're reaching, if you don't feel the ground, it gets really hard.
We all know this.
We've all experienced this.
*Mountains and rivers block your way.*
And mountains and rivers is a famous, famous expression in Zen.
It shows up all the time.
It actually means the landscape or the world.
So the world, everything, blocks your way, the whole world.
Sansui is mountains and rivers.
It's like the name of our temple.
So this temple is the whole world, the whole landscape.
And I love the way the poet's voice comes through at the very end, reaching out to us from somewhere around 750, 740.
Master Shitou says:
*I respectfully urge you who study the mystery, do not pass your days and nights in vain.*
Don't waste this life.
We're here for a reason.
We're here to serve and help.
And I was about to say we're here to bring light, but that's not quite it, right?
We're here to bring light and dark and dark and light.
We're here to heal the optical delusion of consciousness in ourselves and help everyone else heal.
And this has the same kind of tricky, multi-meaning, multi-levels of meaning.
Well, how do I know if I'm passing my days and nights in vain?
One could imagine getting very uptight, very upset, trying so hard.
It's not that either.
So these are all things for us to investigate.
Basically the whole poem is: how do you live in the way that's true, the way that's really true?
And probably whatever we're leaning into is a little bit out of balance, so we're going to keep rebalancing, readjusting.
Light and dark, dark and light.
It's not a long time, but let's use the minutes that we have according to the clock anyway.
Time is another optical delusion, isn't it?
By gathering, as we did last week, let's just do exactly the same, keep things simple.
Find yourself in a group of three.
Take turns speaking and deeply listening.
I won't time it, because there's not a lot of time anyway.
What speaks to you here?
What is the light in your life?
What is the dark in your life?
What did you hear in this discussion, in the poem, about how dark and light can meet in some way?
How does it work for you?
Please find a couple of friends.
Say hi, take a breath, and then say, "Okay, I'll go first.
I don't know what I'm talking about."
And start.
